prompt: Noor, the analytics lead, sets this take-home task on Online Retail II, a public dataset of the invoice lines of a UK online gift shop, and asks how the shop's net product revenue moved through 2010. Take the lines dated from 1 January to 31 December 2010, each in the month of its invoice date. A product line is a line whose stock code starts with a digit; every other code stays out, such as POST, DOT, M or BANK CHARGES for postage, fees, adjustments and vouchers. An invoice whose number starts with C is a cancellation: it counts in the month of its own date, and its quantities are negative. A line's value is its quantity times its price, in pounds sterling, and lines with a missing customer ID count. Both of the source's sheets held some of the same December 2010 lines, and the data keeps one copy of those. A line that matches another line in every column, a missing value matching a missing value, is a copy: count it once. Return one row per month with five columns in this order: month_start, the first day of the month; sales_gbp, the value of the product lines on invoices that are not cancellations; cancelled_gbp, the value of the product lines on cancellations, as a positive amount; net_revenue_gbp, sales_gbp minus cancelled_gbp; and cancelled_pct, 100 times cancelled_gbp divided by sales_gbp, missing when sales_gbp is 0. Round the three amounts to 2 decimals and cancelled_pct to 1 decimal. Sort by month_start from early to late.
hints: Next, keep only the 2010 product lines, with one copy of each repeated line, before you add anything up.
Group the kept lines by month, and split each month's value with a condition on whether the invoice number starts with C.
why_this_works: Removing the copies first counts each sale once, and a condition on the invoice number splits sales from cancellations without losing the lines that have no customer ID.
